To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the discrete ambiguity in the determination of (\ensuremath {\alpha},\ensuremat{beta},\ensuremat {gamma} ) can make the discovery of new physics difficult, but that this ambiguity can usually be resolved.

the discrete ambiguity in (\ensuremath{\beta}-\ensuremath{\pi}) and (\ensuremath{\gamma}-\ensuremath{2}\ensuremath{\pi}+{\ensuremath{\beta}}^{\prime}) can usually be resolved and, if not, the presence of new-physics contributions to these angles can be established; that the discrete ambiguity can be resolved in all cases if one allows for new physics in the B and D systems, but not in the K system; and that
(i) the discrete ambiguity can be resolved in most of the parameter space and (ii) in the remaining part of the parameter space, one can usually still establish the presence of the new physics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how can one be certain that new physics is present in the B and/or K systems?
the question of how to determine if new physics exists in the quark flavor sector and, if so, to what extent it can be constrained.
the question of how well we can determine the CKM parameters from measurements in the B system, and how the presence of new-physics effects can be established.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
if the discrete ambiguity is not resolved, new physics is not ruled out.
the first CP-violation measurements in the B system, if consistent with the SM expectations, would not be able to rule out new physics.
if one of the candidate solutions is consistent, then one can be confident that new physics is absent, but if both are, then one can only say that the data are consistent with new physics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the discrete ambiguity can make it difficult to discover new physics, but it can be overcome by a combination of experimental and theoretical efforts.
the discrete ambiguities can be resolved, but that the resolution of these discrete ambiguities is not sufficient to establish the presence of the new physics.
the discrete ambiguity can usually be resolved in the presence of any new physics.
